pdf-item-equation-3-3.Breakdown.Freq.heatFactor: `Breakdown.Freq.heatFactor` gives $m_t(\xi)=e^{-4\pi^2\max\{t,0\}|\xi|^2}$, agreeing with the multiplier in (3.3) for $t\ge0$. The numbered equation also includes the semigroup identity and the contraction estimate, neither of which is asserted by this scalar definition.
pdf-item-equation-3-3.Breakdown.Freq.heat_holds: $X$ is represented by $g\in L^2(\mathbb R^3;\mathbb C^3)$ with $g(-\xi)=\overline{g(\xi)}$ and $\xi\cdot g(\xi)=0$ almost everywhere. $g=2\pi|\xi|\hat u$ corresponds to a velocity $u$ and $\|g\|_2$ to $\|\nabla u\|_2$. `Breakdown.Freq.heat_holds` gives the multiplier $G(t)g=e^{-4\pi^2t|\xi|^2}g$ for $t\ge0$, $G(s+t)=G(s)G(t)$ for $s,t\ge0$, and $\|G(t)g\|_2\le\|g\|_2$. These supply all three clauses of (3.3). It additionally proves $G(0)=I$, strong continuity and self-adjointness.

pdf-item-equation-3-4.Breakdown.dilateField: For any field $u$ and $\mu>0$, the definition is $D_\mu u(x)=\sqrt\mu u(\sqrt\mu x)$, the first formula of (3.4). Its extension is zero for $\mu\le0$. It does not define the orthogonal action in the second formula.
pdf-item-equation-3-4.Breakdown.pushForward: For any $R\in O(3)$ and field $u$, the definition is $\rho_Ru(x)=Ru(R^{-1}x)$, the second formula of (3.4). It includes reflections and imposes no regularity. It does not define the dilation in the first formula.

ns-s3-actions-on-space.Breakdown.Freq.velocityCov_holds: `Breakdown.Freq.velocityCov_holds` identifies the physical velocity of $Rg(R^{-1}\xi)$ with $R\,u(R^{-1}x)$ almost everywhere, and the velocity of $\mu^{-1/2}g(\xi/\sqrt\mu)$ with $\sqrt\mu\,u(\sqrt\mu x)$ almost everywhere for $\mu>0$. Both frequency transformations are operators on $X$. This supplies the physical interpretation of the two actions in the paper.

pdf-item-equation-3-5.Breakdown.Freq.dilation_holds:
$X$ is represented by $g\in L^2(\mathbb R^3;\mathbb C^3)$ with $g(-\xi)=\overline{g(\xi)}$ and $\xi\cdot g(\xi)=0$ almost everywhere. $g=2\pi|\xi|\hat u$ corresponds to a velocity $u$ and $\|g\|_2$ to $\|
abla u\|_2$. For $\mu,
u>0$ and $t\ge0$, `Breakdown.Freq.dilation_holds` gives $\|D_\mu g\|_2=\mu^{1/4}\|g\|_2$, $D_{\mu
u}=D_\mu D_
u$ and $D_\mu G(\mu t)=G(t)D_\mu$. Here $D_\mu g(\xi)=\mu^{-1/2}g(\xi/\sqrt\mu)$ and $G(t)$ is the Gaussian heat multiplier. These are all three clauses of (3.5), with real exponent $1/4$.

ns-s3-projected-heat-forcing.Breakdown.Freq.heatDivFree: `Breakdown.Freq.heatDivFree` defines the projected heat evolution of an $L^2$ source using the heat multiplier and the orthogonal solenoidal projection. The $L^{3/2}$ domain and the corresponding $\tau^{-3/4}$ bound in (3.6) require a separate estimate.
ns-s3-projected-heat-forcing.Breakdown.Freq.bilin_holds: For all $\tau>0$ and $u,v\in X=\dot H^1_{\mathrm{div}}$, `Breakdown.Freq.bilin_holds` supplies the bounded bilinear map $K(\tau):X\times X\to X$ and one constant in $\|K(\tau)(u,v)\|_X\le C_K\tau^{-3/4}\|u\|_X\|v\|_X$. This proves the bilinear conclusion (3.7), but Lemma 3.1 also gives the linear estimate for every $L^{3/2}$ force.
ns-s3-projected-heat-forcing.Breakdown.Freq.bilinShift_holds: For $u,v\in X=\dot H^1_{\mathrm{div}}(\mathbb R^3)$, $t\ge0$ and $\tau>0$, `Breakdown.Freq.bilinShift_holds` gives $e^{t\Delta}K(\tau)(u,v)=K(t+\tau)(u,v)$, where $K(\tau)(u,v)=-\tfrac12e^{\tau\Delta}\mathbb P[(u\cdot\nabla)v+(v\cdot\nabla)u]$. The paper states a heat-shift identity and continuity for every $L^{3/2}$ force. It supplies the identity only for the bilinear forcing class.
ns-s3-projected-heat-forcing.Breakdown.Freq.bilinCont_holds: For each fixed pair $u,v\in X=\dot H^1_{\mathrm{div}}(\mathbb R^3)$, `Breakdown.Freq.bilinCont_holds` proves continuity of $\tau\mapsto K(\tau)(u,v)$ on $(0,\infty)$ in the homogeneous $H^1$ norm. The paper permits any $L^{3/2}$ forcing field and also states the heat-shift identity. Neither extension is part of this continuity theorem.

ns-s3-forcing-time-properties.Breakdown.Freq.bilinShift_holds: For $u,v\in X=\dot H^1_{\mathrm{div}}(\mathbb R^3)$, $t\ge0$ and $\tau>0$, `Breakdown.Freq.bilinShift_holds` gives $e^{t\Delta}K(\tau)(u,v)=K(t+\tau)(u,v)$, where $K(\tau)(u,v)=-\tfrac12e^{\tau\Delta}\mathbb P[(u\cdot\nabla)v+(v\cdot\nabla)u]$. The paper states a heat-shift identity and continuity for every $L^{3/2}$ force. It supplies the identity only for the bilinear forcing class.
ns-s3-forcing-time-properties.Breakdown.Freq.bilinCont_holds: For each fixed pair $u,v\in X=\dot H^1_{\mathrm{div}}(\mathbb R^3)$, `Breakdown.Freq.bilinCont_holds` proves continuity of $\tau\mapsto K(\tau)(u,v)$ on $(0,\infty)$ in the homogeneous $H^1$ norm. The paper permits any $L^{3/2}$ forcing field and also states the heat-shift identity. Neither extension is part of this continuity theorem.

ns-s3-bilinear-existence.Breakdown.Freq.bilin_holds: `Breakdown.Freq.bilin_holds` constructs the symmetric bilinear term for positive lag and proves its $\tau^{-3/4}$ bound in $X$. The map is characterized by pairing with represented test velocities, as in the bilinear part of Lemma 3.1.

pdf-item-equation-3-7.Breakdown.Freq.bilin_holds: `Breakdown.Freq.bilin_holds` proves that one $C_K\ge0$, independent of $\tau,u,v$, satisfies $\|K(\tau)(u,v)\|_X\le C_K\tau^{-3/4}\|u\|_X\|v\|_X$ for every $\tau>0$ and $u,v\in X$. Here $X$ is the solenoidal homogeneous $H^1$ space in its Fourier representation, and $K$ is the symmetric projected advection term of (2.3). The exponent is a real exponent and the norm is $\|\nabla u\|_2$, as in (3.7).

adapted.N2-03.1.Breakdown.Freq.bilin_holds: For positive lag $\tau$, `Breakdown.Freq.bilin_holds` constructs the bilinear term on the homogeneous space and bounds it by a constant times $\tau^{-3/4}\|u\|_X\|v\|_X$. This is (3.7). The more general source estimate (3.6) has a separate input class.

pdf-item-equation-3-8.Breakdown.Freq.bilinShift_holds: For $u,v\in X=\dot H^1_{\mathrm{div}}(\mathbb R^3)$, $t\ge0$ and $\tau>0$, `Breakdown.Freq.bilinShift_holds` gives $e^{t\Delta}K(\tau)(u,v)=K(t+\tau)(u,v)$ in the Fourier representation of $X$. The two bilinear lags are positive. This is the first identity of (3.8), for the symmetric projected advection term $K$ of (2.3). This supplies the first of the three identities in the numbered display.
pdf-item-equation-3-8.Breakdown.Freq.bilinDilate_holds: For all $\mu,\tau>0$ and $u,v\in X=\dot H^1_{\mathrm{div}}(\mathbb R^3)$, `Breakdown.Freq.bilinDilate_holds` gives $\mu D_\mu K(\mu\tau)(u,v)=K(\tau)(D_\mu u,D_\mu v)$, with $D_\mu u(x)=\sqrt\mu\,u(\sqrt\mu x)$. The equality is in the Fourier representation of $X$ and agrees with the second identity of (3.8), including the factor $\mu$. This supplies its dilation identity. The heat-shift and orthogonal identities are separate.
pdf-item-equation-3-8.Breakdown.Freq.bilinRotate_holds: For every $R\in O(3)$, real $\tau$ and $u,v\in X=\dot H^1_{\mathrm{div}}(\mathbb R^3)$, `Breakdown.Freq.bilinRotate_holds` gives $\rho_RK(\tau)(u,v)=K(\tau)(\rho_Ru,\rho_Rv)$, where $\rho_Ru(x)=Ru(R^{-1}x)$. For $\tau>0$ this is the last identity of (3.8), for $\tau\le0$ the formal bilinear map is zero. Reflections are included. On the paper’s positive-time domain, this supplies its orthogonal identity. The other two identities are separate.

ns-s3-projection-homogeneity.Breakdown.Freq.Internal.Dilation.longitu: `Breakdown.Freq.Internal.Dilation.longitudinal_smul` is written for the complementary longitudinal projection and every nonzero real scaling. Subtracting it from it gives exactly the paper’s degree-zero homogeneity.

ns-s3-projection-covariance.Breakdown.Freq.Internal.Rotation.longitu: `Breakdown.Freq.Internal.Rotation.longitudinal_rotC` is for the longitudinal projection. A change of the frequency variable and subtraction from it give the displayed solenoidal covariance, including reflections.

adapted.N2-04.1.Breakdown.FarField.kernelL1Bound_holds: `Breakdown.FarField.kernelL1Bound_holds` establishes integrability of the differentiated projected heat kernel at positive time. The $L^1$ bound enables convolution estimates for the bilinear term.

ns-s3-oseen-decay.Breakdown.FarField.lerayKernelBound_hold: `Breakdown.FarField.lerayKernelBound_holds` is $|\partial_k(O_\tau)_{ij}(x)|\le C(|x|+\sqrt\tau)^{-4}$, with one constant for all indices. It supplies $l=1$ componentwise and no all-order estimate.

adapted.N2-04.2.Breakdown.FarField.lerayKernelBound_hold: `Breakdown.FarField.lerayKernelBound_holds` gives the fourth-power spatial decay for one derivative of the projected heat kernel. That is the case of the derivative bound needed here.

ns-s3-oseen-scaling.Breakdown.FarField.kernelScaling_holds: Writing $G_\tau$ for the Gaussian heat kernel and $H_{ijk}(\tau,x)$ for the Gaussian-integral representation of $\partial_k(O_\tau)_{ij}$, `Breakdown.FarField.kernelScaling_holds` proves $G_{\mu\tau}(\sqrt\mu x)=\mu^{-3/2}G_\tau(x)$ and $H_{ijk}(\mu\tau,\sqrt\mu x)=\mu^{-2}H_{ijk}(\tau,x)$ for $\mu,\tau>0$. It states no scaling identity for $O_\tau$ itself, which is the object in the paper’s quoted formula.

ns-s3-oseen-lp-scaling.Breakdown.FarField.kernelScaling_holds: For $\mu,\tau>0$, `Breakdown.FarField.kernelScaling_holds` proves the pointwise identity $\partial_k(O_{\mu\tau})_{ij}(\sqrt\mu x)=\mu^{-2}\partial_k(O_\tau)_{ij}(x)$ for the explicitly defined derivative kernel. A change of variables and finiteness of the $L^p$ norms give the paper’s norm identity. It contains neither a quantifier over $p$ nor that norm calculation.
ns-s3-oseen-lp-scaling.Breakdown.FarField.kernelL1Bound_holds: `Breakdown.FarField.kernelL1Bound_holds` proves integrability and $\int|\partial_k(O_\tau)_{ij}|\le C\tau^{-1/2}$ for every $\tau>0$ and each coordinate triple. This gives a finite componentwise $L^1$ bound. The paper’s sentence gives an exact norm-scaling equality for every $1\le p\le\infty$, so it covers only part of it.

ns-s3-derivative-convolution-definition.Breakdown.FarField.kernelConv: For any real matrix field $F$ on $\mathbb R^3$, `Breakdown.FarField.kernelConv` has component $\int_{\mathbb R^3}\sum_{j,m}\partial_m(O_\tau)_{ij}(y-z)F_{jm}(z)\,dz$, with the derivative kernel defined by its Gaussian formula. If the component terms are integrable, this is exactly $(\nabla O_\tau*F)_i$ in §3.2. It imposes no integrability. A nonintegrable component integral is assigned zero.

ns-s3-tensor-product.Breakdown.FarField.tensorField: `Breakdown.FarField.tensorField` has the same ordered pair of vector components in each matrix entry and places no additional conditions on the two fields.

ns-s3-convolution-mixed-inputs.Breakdown.FarField.BilinKernel: For $\tau>0$ and $g\in X=\dot H^1_{\mathrm{div}}(\mathbb R^3)$ in its Fourier representation, let $u$ be the reconstructed $L^6$ velocity. `Breakdown.FarField.BilinKernel` is that the velocity of $K(\tau)(g,g)$ equals $-\nabla O_\tau*(u\otimes u)$ almost everywhere. It states the diagonal part of (3.10). Bilinearity and polarization are needed to obtain the displayed formula for distinct inputs. It states this condition. It does not prove it.
ns-s3-convolution-mixed-inputs.Breakdown.FarField.bilinKernel_of_test_d: The matrix norm in this hypothesis is the maximum absolute entry. It then gives the diagonal identity for every represented $\dot H^1$ input, almost everywhere in space. The paper’s formula has two independent inputs. Polarization is an additional deduction from this diagonal conclusion.

ns-s3-compact-monodromy.Breakdown.MonodromyStatement: For a subdivision into $k\ge1$ pieces on which each linearized Duhamel operator has norm at most $1/4$, it states that the period operator $M$ differs compactly from its free heat-and-dilation counterpart $M_0$, and $\|M_0\|\le e^{-S/4}<1$. This specifies the monodromy conclusion mentioned in the paper. It is a definition of an assertion, and it assumes the smallness of the chosen subdivision.

ns-s3-compactness-lemma.Breakdown.Freq.bilinCompact_holds: For $\tau>0$ and $u$ in the real linear span of represented $C^\infty_{c,\mathrm{div}}(\mathbb R^3)$ fields, `Breakdown.Freq.bilinCompact_holds` proves that $v\mapsto K(\tau)(u,v)$ is compact on the solenoidal homogeneous $H^1$ space. Lemma 3.2 allows every $u\in X$. Extending the first-input quantifier requires density, bounded bilinearity and closure of compact operators in operator norm. Those steps are not the conclusion of this linked theorem.

ns-s3-compactness-advection-formula.Breakdown.Freq.bilinTestFormula_holds: For $\tau>0$, $\varphi\in C^\infty_{c,\mathrm{div}}(\mathbb R^3)$ and $v\in X=\dot H^1_{\mathrm{div}}(\mathbb R^3)$, `Breakdown.Freq.bilinTestFormula_holds` states $K(\tau)(\varphi,v)=-\tfrac12e^{\tau\Delta}\mathbb P[(\varphi\cdot\nabla)v+(v\cdot\nabla)\varphi]$ in the frequency representation. The bracket belongs to $L^2$ and equals $\operatorname{div}(\varphi\otimes v+v\otimes\varphi)$. This gives the displayed formula with $F_v=\varphi\otimes v+v\otimes\varphi$.

adapted.N2-05.1.Breakdown.Freq.bilinCompact_holds: `Breakdown.Freq.bilinCompact_holds` proves compactness at fixed positive lag with the first input in the span of embedded test fields. This is the starting case for the approximation argument. The paper explains it using local Rellich compactness.

adapted.N2-06.1.Breakdown.HeatBilinear: `Breakdown.HeatBilinear` packages symmetric bounded bilinear maps at positive lag with a strongly continuous contraction semigroup, the heat time-shift law and a $\tau^{-3/4}$ bound for $0<\tau\le1$. The paper writes the bound for all positive lags.

pdf-item-equation-3-11.Breakdown.HeatBilinear: On a real normed space $\mathcal X$, the formal assumptions include $G(0)=I$, $G(s+t)=G(s)G(t)$ for $s,t\ge0$, and $\|G(t)\|\le1$ for $t\ge0$. Thus $\|G(t)u\|\le\|u\|$, as in (3.11), with $G(t)=e^{t\Delta}$ in the paper. Values at negative times are defined but these heat-flow laws are imposed only on nonnegative times.

pdf-item-equation-3-12.Breakdown.HeatBilinear: The formal assumptions give $G(t)K(\tau)(u,v)=K(t+\tau)(u,v)$ for $t\ge0,\tau>0$ and all $u,v$ in a real normed space. They require $\|K(\tau)(u,v)\|\le C_K\tau^{-3/4}\|u\|\|v\|$ only for $0<\tau\le1$. Equation (3.12) contains both clauses and requires the power bound for every $\tau>0$. Thus the full numbered comparison is weaker, although the isolated shift clause agrees.

ns-3late-abstract-mild.Breakdown.HeatBilinear.IsMildOn: For a real normed space with the stipulated $G,K$, the formal half-open condition requires $u:\mathbb R\to\mathcal X$ to be continuous on $[a,b)$ and, for each $a\le t<b$, requires Bochner integrability and $u(t)=G(t-a)u(a)+\int_a^tK(t-s)(u(s),u(s))\,ds$. This is (2.4) on that interval. Values outside it and the single integrand value at $s=t$ do not affect the condition.
ns-3late-abstract-mild.Breakdown.HeatBilinear.IsMildOnIcc: For a real normed space with the stipulated $G,K$, the formal closed-interval condition requires continuity on $[a,b]$ and, for every $t\in[a,b]$, Bochner integrability and $u(t)=G(t-a)u(a)+\int_a^tK(t-s)(u(s),u(s))\,ds$. Both endpoints are included, as in the closed-interval version of (2.4). No conditions are imposed outside $[a,b]$.

ns-3late-lemma-3-3.Breakdown.VarConstIntegralStatement: `Breakdown.VarConstIntegralStatement` states that the Duhamel integral exists in the Bochner sense and is continuous for continuous inputs on the closed interval. With the positive-lag norm bound on $0<\tau\le1$, it also specifies the short-interval factor $4C_K(t-a)^{1/4}$ times the two input suprema.
ns-3late-lemma-3-3.Breakdown.varConstIntegral: `Breakdown.varConstIntegral` proves existence and time continuity of the Bochner integral in Lemma 3.3. Its kernel estimate is needed only for lags at most one, and gives a bound by $4C_K(t-a)^{1/4}$ times the supremum norms of the inputs for $t-a\le1$.

ns-3late-lemma-3-4-equation.Breakdown.PieceOperatorStatement: For $T>0$, `Breakdown.PieceOperatorStatement` identifies $B_T:C([0,T];\mathcal X)^2\to C([0,T];\mathcal X)$ by $B_T(f,h)(t)=\int_0^tK(t-s)(f(s),h(s))\,ds$ and proves bounded bilinearity. $\|B_T\|\le4C_KT^{1/4}$ when $T\le1$. It also identifies $\Gamma_T:\mathcal X\to C([0,T];\mathcal X)$ by $\Gamma_Tx(t)=G(t)x$, with norm at most one. Translating time gives the integral operator in Lemma 3.4. Invertibility of $I-2B_T(f,\cdot)$ on an arbitrary interval is a further conclusion. It states these operator properties.
ns-3late-lemma-3-4-equation.Breakdown.pieceOperator: For $T>0$, `Breakdown.pieceOperator` identifies $B_T:C([0,T];\mathcal X)^2\to C([0,T];\mathcal X)$ by $B_T(f,h)(t)=\int_0^tK(t-s)(f(s),h(s))\,ds$ and proves bounded bilinearity. $\|B_T\|\le4C_KT^{1/4}$ when $T\le1$. It also identifies $\Gamma_T:\mathcal X\to C([0,T];\mathcal X)$ by $\Gamma_Tx(t)=G(t)x$, with norm at most one. Translating time gives the integral operator in Lemma 3.4. Invertibility of $I-2B_T(f,\cdot)$ on an arbitrary interval is a further conclusion. It proves these operator properties.
ns-3late-lemma-3-4-equation.Breakdown.Periodic.InverseAlgebra.Intern: For a bounded operator $A$ on a real Banach space with $\|A\|<1$, `Breakdown.Periodic.InverseAlgebra.Internal.sub_apply_inverse_one_sub` gives $h-Ah=g$ for $h=(I-A)^{-1}g$ and every $g$. Taking $A h(t)=2\int_a^tK(t-s)(f(s),h(s))\,ds$ requires a separate smallness estimate in this norm. Lemma 3.4 asserts invertibility of this Volterra equation for every continuous $f$ and every finite interval, without that norm-smallness assumption.

ns-3late-lemma-3-4-bound.Breakdown.Periodic.InverseAlgebra.Intern: For a bounded operator $A$ on a real Banach space and $\|A\|\le q<1$, `Breakdown.Periodic.InverseAlgebra.Internal.norm_inverse_one_sub_le` proves $\|(I-A)^{-1}\|\le(1-q)^{-1}$. The paper’s sentence concerns the solution operator of $h(t)=2\int_a^tK(t-s)(f(s),h(s))\,ds+g(t)$ on any finite $[a,b]$. It imposes no smallness of the Volterra operator in the supremum norm. The linked inverse estimate requires that additional hypothesis.

pdf-item-theorem-3-5.Breakdown.RestrictStatement: If its quadratic Duhamel integrals are Bochner integrable and $u(r)=G(r-a)u(a)+\int_a^rK(r-s)(u(s),u(s))\,ds$ holds for $r=m,t$, `Breakdown.RestrictStatement` gives Bochner integrability on $[m,t]$ and $u(t)=G(t-m)u(m)+\int_m^tK(t-s)(u(s),u(s))\,ds$. Formula (3.13) permits independent factors $f,h$ and assumes the original identity throughout an interval. The formal implication uses the quadratic factors $u,u$ and only two times. This linked definition states the implication.
pdf-item-theorem-3-5.Breakdown.restrict: If its quadratic Duhamel integrals are Bochner integrable and $u(r)=G(r-a)u(a)+\int_a^rK(r-s)(u(s),u(s))\,ds$ holds for $r=m,t$, `Breakdown.restrict` gives Bochner integrability on $[m,t]$ and $u(t)=G(t-m)u(m)+\int_m^tK(t-s)(u(s),u(s))\,ds$. Formula (3.13) permits independent factors $f,h$ and assumes the original identity throughout an interval. The formal implication uses the quadratic factors $u,u$ and only two times. This linked theorem proves it.
pdf-item-theorem-3-5.Breakdown.UniqueStatement: `Breakdown.UniqueStatement` also gives this conclusion on $[a,b)$ and imposes no smallness of the datum or interval. It includes the uniqueness clause of Lemma 3.5 under a kernel estimate required only at lags at most one. It supplies the uniqueness clause only. The same numbered lemma also has a restart identity with independent factors $f,h$.
pdf-item-theorem-3-5.Breakdown.mildUnique: `Breakdown.mildUnique` also gives this conclusion on $[a,b)$ and imposes no smallness of the datum or interval. It includes the uniqueness clause of Lemma 3.5 under a kernel estimate required only at lags at most one. It proves the uniqueness clause. It does not prove the same lemma’s general-factor restart formula.

pdf-item-equation-3-13.Breakdown.RestrictStatement: If its quadratic Duhamel integrals are Bochner integrable and $u(r)=G(r-a)u(a)+\int_a^rK(r-s)(u(s),u(s))\,ds$ holds for $r=m,t$, `Breakdown.RestrictStatement` gives Bochner integrability on $[m,t]$ and $u(t)=G(t-m)u(m)+\int_m^tK(t-s)(u(s),u(s))\,ds$. Formula (3.13) permits independent factors $f,h$ and assumes the original identity throughout an interval. The formal implication uses the quadratic factors $u,u$ and only two times. This linked definition states the implication.
pdf-item-equation-3-13.Breakdown.restrict: If its quadratic Duhamel integrals are Bochner integrable and $u(r)=G(r-a)u(a)+\int_a^rK(r-s)(u(s),u(s))\,ds$ holds for $r=m,t$, `Breakdown.restrict` gives Bochner integrability on $[m,t]$ and $u(t)=G(t-m)u(m)+\int_m^tK(t-s)(u(s),u(s))\,ds$. Formula (3.13) permits independent factors $f,h$ and assumes the original identity throughout an interval. The formal implication uses the quadratic factors $u,u$ and only two times. This linked theorem proves it.

ns-3late-lemma-3-5-unique.Breakdown.UniqueStatement: `Breakdown.UniqueStatement` also gives this conclusion on $[a,b)$ and imposes no smallness of the datum or interval. It includes the uniqueness clause of Lemma 3.5 under a kernel estimate required only at lags at most one.
ns-3late-lemma-3-5-unique.Breakdown.mildUnique: `Breakdown.mildUnique` also gives this conclusion on $[a,b)$ and imposes no smallness of the datum or interval. It includes the uniqueness clause of Lemma 3.5 under a kernel estimate required only at lags at most one. This linked theorem proves it.

ns-3late-restart-consequence.Breakdown.restrict: If $u$ is a continuous mild solution on $[a,b]$ and $a\le m<b$, the formal restart implication applied at each $t\in[m,b]$ gives $u(t)=G(t-m)u(m)+\int_m^tK(t-s)(u(s),u(s))\,ds$ with Bochner integrability. Thus $u$ is mild on $[m,b]$, exactly as in this explicitly quadratic specialization of (3.13).

adapted.N2-07.2.Breakdown.Freq.mild_holds: `Breakdown.Freq.mild_holds` gives the mild identity on the closed interval, including $b$, under the frequency-space weak-solution assumptions. Those assumptions include spatial regularity beyond the paper’s continuous $X$-valued curve premise.

ns-3late-weak-assumptions.Breakdown.Freq.IsWeakSolution:
The represented curve is continuous in $X$. Every slice difference lies in $L^2$ and tends to zero in $L^2$ as the times approach one another. For each smooth compactly supported solenoidal $\psi$, the pairing $\int v(t)\cdot\psi$ is continuous on $[a,b]$ and has derivative $-\int
abla v(t):
abla\psi-\int((v(t)\cdot
abla)v(t))\cdot\psi$ on $(a,b)$. The constants $C_t$ need not be uniform. Lemma 3.6 permits any continuous $X=\dot H^1_{\mathrm{div}}$ curve and requires continuously differentiable pairings up to both endpoints. `Breakdown.Freq.IsWeakSolution` therefore strengthens the spatial and difference hypotheses while requiring test-pairing derivatives only in the open interval.
ns-3late-weak-assumptions.Breakdown.Freq.MildOfWeak: Lemma 3.6 uses arbitrary continuous $X$-valued curves with endpoint-inclusive continuously differentiable test pairings. Its hypotheses differ in both spatial regularity and time endpoints. `Breakdown.Freq.MildOfWeak` states the implication for the stated stronger spatial class.
ns-3late-weak-assumptions.Breakdown.Freq.mild_holds: Lemma 3.6 uses arbitrary continuous $X$-valued curves with endpoint-inclusive continuously differentiable test pairings. Its hypotheses differ in both spatial regularity and time endpoints. `Breakdown.Freq.mild_holds` proves the implication for that class.

ns-3late-weak-equation.Breakdown.Freq.IsWeakSolution: The pressure disappears against solenoidal tests and the weak pairing contains the diffusion and transport terms from (3.14). The Lean time derivative is imposed in the interior $a<t<b$, with additional spatial decay and $L^2$ difference assumptions.

ns-3late-tensor-contraction.Breakdown.advectionPairing: `Breakdown.advectionPairing` is $\int_{\mathbb R^3}((u\cdot\nabla)u)\cdot\psi\,dx$. For smooth solenoidal $u$ and a smooth compactly supported $\psi$, its negative equals $\int\sum_{i,j}u_i u_j\partial_i\psi_j\,dx$ by integration by parts. The paper defines a general three-field tensor contraction. It instead gives this two-field transport pairing and does not assert the integration-by-parts theorem.

ns-3late-weak-to-mild.Breakdown.Freq.MildOfWeak: Lemma 3.6 uses arbitrary continuous $X$-valued curves with endpoint-inclusive continuously differentiable test pairings. Its hypotheses differ in both spatial regularity and time endpoints. This linked definition states the implication.
ns-3late-weak-to-mild.Breakdown.Freq.mild_holds: Lemma 3.6 uses arbitrary continuous $X$-valued curves with endpoint-inclusive continuously differentiable test pairings. Its hypotheses differ in both spatial regularity and time endpoints. This linked theorem proves it.

pdf-item-equation-3-15.Breakdown.Periodic.V: The formal periodic space consists of real solenoidal fields of period one with norm $\|u\|_{H^1}^2=\sum_{n\in\mathbb Z^3}(1+4\pi^2|n|^2)|\hat u(n)|^2$. The mean may be nonzero. The coefficient at $n=0$ contributes $|\hat u(0)|^2$. Equation (3.15) instead has $L^3\sum_{k\in L^{-1}\mathbb Z^3}4\pi^2|k|^2|\hat u(k)|^2$ on mean-zero fields.
pdf-item-equation-3-15.Breakdown.Periodic.weight: The formal weight is $w(n)=1+4\pi^2|n|^2$ for $n\in\mathbb Z^3$. Therefore $\sum_nw(n)|\hat u(n)|^2$ includes the $L^2$ term and the mean, unlike the homogeneous weight $4\pi^2|k|^2$ in (3.15), with its variable-period normalization.
pdf-item-equation-3-15.Breakdown.Periodic.norm_sq_eq_tsum: The formal periodic space consists of real solenoidal fields of period one with norm $\|u\|_{H^1}^2=\sum_{n\in\mathbb Z^3}(1+4\pi^2|n|^2)|\hat u(n)|^2$. The mean may be nonzero. `Breakdown.Periodic.norm_sq_eq_tsum` proves this coefficient identity for every element of that space, whose weighted coefficients are square summable. It has neither the $L^3$ volume factor nor frequencies $n/L$ of (3.15), and the mean is unrestricted.

pdf-item-equation-3-16.Breakdown.Periodic.weight: `Breakdown.Periodic.weight` gives $w(n)=1+4\pi^2|n|^2$. It supplies no norm-equivalence theorem. For mean-zero coefficients, $|n|\ge1$ on the remaining frequencies gives $\|u\|_{\dot H^1}\le\|u\|_{H^1}\le(1+(4\pi^2)^{-1})^{1/2}\|u\|_{\dot H^1}$ at period one, without mean zero this fails for constants.
pdf-item-equation-3-16.Breakdown.Periodic.norm_sq_eq_tsum: The formal periodic space consists of real solenoidal fields of period one with norm $\|u\|_{H^1}^2=\sum_{n\in\mathbb Z^3}(1+4\pi^2|n|^2)|\hat u(n)|^2$. The mean may be nonzero. `Breakdown.Periodic.norm_sq_eq_tsum` establishes the inhomogeneous coefficient identity. Equation (3.16) additionally restricts $\hat u(0)=0$ and compares this norm with $(\sum_n4\pi^2|n|^2|\hat u(n)|^2)^{1/2}$. That implication requires the mean-zero restriction and comparison of weights and is not it’s conclusion.

ns-3late-periodic-heat-multiplier.Breakdown.Periodic.heat: The formal operator multiplies each Fourier coefficient by $\exp(-4\pi^2\max\{t,0\}|n|^2)$. For $t\ge0$ this agrees with the paper’s multiplier at period one. Negative parameters give the identity. The paper quantifies over every period $L>0$ and uses the homogeneous mean-zero space.

ns-3late-periodic-force.Breakdown.Periodic.forceV: For $\tau>0$, the formal construction gives the Fourier coefficient $e^{-4\pi^2\tau|n|^2}\mathbb P_n\hat f(n)$, with $\hat f$ integrated over $[0,1]^3$ and $\mathbb P_0=I$. For $f\in L^1([0,1]^3)$ this is the paper’s projected heat field at $L=1$. Outside that integrability class Fourier integrals are assigned zero. The construction includes no arbitrary spatial period.

pdf-item-equation-3-17.Breakdown.Periodic.kernel: For $\tau>0$, the formal operator is the Fourier-series form of $-\tfrac12e^{\tau\Delta}\mathbb P[(u\cdot\nabla)v+(v\cdot\nabla)u]$. It has the same symmetrization and sign as (3.17) at $L=1$, but acts on the larger space permitting constants, for $\tau\le0$ it is zero. The paper uses the homogeneous mean-zero space for every period.
pdf-item-equation-3-17.Breakdown.Periodic.kernel_symm: `Breakdown.Periodic.kernel_symm` proves only $K_{\mathbb T}(\tau)(u,v)=K_{\mathbb T}(\tau)(v,u)$ for all real $\tau$ and all inputs, with both sides zero for $\tau\le0$. This symmetry follows from the symmetrization in (3.17). The theorem does not state that whole physical formula or quantify over spatial periods.

ns-3late-periodic-mild.Breakdown.Periodic.IsMildOn: For a curve $u$ defined for all real times, the condition is continuity on the indicated interval and $u(t)=e^{(t-a)\Delta}u(a)+\int_a^tK_{\mathbb T}(t-s)(u(s),u(s))\,ds$ there, with Bochner integrability for every such $t$. `Breakdown.Periodic.IsMildOn` uses $a\le t<b$. It has the paper’s half-open Duhamel formula, with a different norm, unrestricted mean and fixed period one.
ns-3late-periodic-mild.Breakdown.Periodic.IsMildOnIcc: For a curve $u$ defined for all real times, the condition is continuity on the indicated interval and $u(t)=e^{(t-a)\Delta}u(a)+\int_a^tK_{\mathbb T}(t-s)(u(s),u(s))\,ds$ there, with Bochner integrability for every such $t$. `Breakdown.Periodic.IsMildOnIcc` uses $a\le t\le b$ and includes both endpoints. It has the paper’s closed-interval formula, with a different norm, unrestricted mean and fixed period one.

ns-3late-periodic-heat-laws.Breakdown.Periodic.heat_zero: The formal periodic space consists of real solenoidal fields of period one with norm $\|u\|_{H^1}^2=\sum_{n\in\mathbb Z^3}(1+4\pi^2|n|^2)|\hat u(n)|^2$. The mean may be nonzero. `Breakdown.Periodic.heat_zero` gives $G(0)=I$, where $G(t)$ multiplies by $e^{-4\pi^2\max\{t,0\}|n|^2}$. This supplies the zero-time identity among the paper’s listed heat properties, at period one.
ns-3late-periodic-heat-laws.Breakdown.Periodic.heat_add: The formal periodic space consists of real solenoidal fields of period one with norm $\|u\|_{H^1}^2=\sum_{n\in\mathbb Z^3}(1+4\pi^2|n|^2)|\hat u(n)|^2$. The mean may be nonzero. For $s,t\ge0$, `Breakdown.Periodic.heat_add` proves $G(s+t)=G(s)G(t)$ for the Gaussian coefficient multipliers. It supplies this part of the paper’s heat laws at period one, with no assertion for arbitrary $L$.
ns-3late-periodic-heat-laws.Breakdown.Periodic.norm_heat_le: The formal periodic space consists of real solenoidal fields of period one with norm $\|u\|_{H^1}^2=\sum_{n\in\mathbb Z^3}(1+4\pi^2|n|^2)|\hat u(n)|^2$. The mean may be nonzero. `Breakdown.Periodic.norm_heat_le` gives $\|G(t)\|\le1$ for all real $t$. Positive times use the Gaussian heat multiplier, and negative times use the assigned identity. The paper states contraction in homogeneous mean-zero spaces for every spatial period.
ns-3late-periodic-heat-laws.Breakdown.Periodic.heat_continuousOn: The formal periodic space consists of real solenoidal fields of period one with norm $\|u\|_{H^1}^2=\sum_{n\in\mathbb Z^3}(1+4\pi^2|n|^2)|\hat u(n)|^2$. The mean may be nonzero. `Breakdown.Periodic.heat_continuousOn` proves continuity of $t\mapsto G(t)u$ in this norm for each fixed input on $[0,\infty)$. The paper states the corresponding strong continuity for its homogeneous mean-zero space at every period.

s3-periodic-sobolev-proof-dependency.Breakdown.Periodic.kernelSharpBound_hold: The formal proof obtains the periodic bilinear bound from a Sobolev estimate through a trilinear estimate. Its Sobolev estimate uses finite Fourier sums and the inhomogeneous unit-torus norm. The following paper display concerns all mean-zero fields with the homogeneous norm at arbitrary period.

pdf-item-equation-3-18.Breakdown.Periodic.TrigHs: There is one $C>0$ such that every finite Fourier sum $p(x)=\sum_{n\in F}e^{2\pi i n\cdot x}c_n$, $c_n\in\mathbb C^3$, obeys $\|p\|_{L^6([0,1]^3)}\le C(\sum_{n\in F}(1+4\pi^2|n|^2)|c_n|^2)^{1/2}$. No reality, solenoidality or mean-zero hypothesis is imposed. Equation (3.18) instead concerns all mean-zero fields, with a homogeneous gradient norm and one constant for every period $L>0$. `Breakdown.Periodic.TrigHs` states this finite-sum assertion.
pdf-item-equation-3-18.Breakdown.Periodic.trigHs: There is one $C>0$ such that every finite Fourier sum $p(x)=\sum_{n\in F}e^{2\pi i n\cdot x}c_n$, $c_n\in\mathbb C^3$, obeys $\|p\|_{L^6([0,1]^3)}\le C(\sum_{n\in F}(1+4\pi^2|n|^2)|c_n|^2)^{1/2}$. No reality, solenoidality or mean-zero hypothesis is imposed. Equation (3.18) instead concerns all mean-zero fields, with a homogeneous gradient norm and one constant for every period $L>0$. `Breakdown.Periodic.trigHs` proves this finite-sum assertion. Extension and period scaling are additional steps.

pdf-item-theorem-3-7.Breakdown.Periodic.ShellTorus.Internal.s: `Breakdown.Periodic.ShellTorus.Internal.sourceOp_threeHalves` gives $\|e^{\mu\tau\Delta}\mathbb P f_\mu\|_{H^1(\mathbb T^3)}\le C\mu^{1/4}\tau^{-3/4}\|A\|_{3/2}$ with one $C$. Compact support makes this $L^{3/2}$ norm finite. Equation (3.19) allows all mean-zero $L^{3/2}$ forces, all periods and all positive times. It uses the homogeneous norm. This comparison covers the linear estimate. The lemma also states shift, continuity and a bilinear estimate.
pdf-item-theorem-3-7.Breakdown.Periodic.Forced.Internal.force: For any field $f:\mathbb R^3\to\mathbb R^3$ and $0<\sigma\le\tau$, `Breakdown.Periodic.Forced.Internal.forceV_eq_heat` gives $F(\tau)=G(\tau-\sigma)F(\sigma)$, where $\widehat{F(r)}(n)=e^{-4\pi^2r|n|^2}\mathbb P_n\hat f(n)$ for $r>0$ and $\hat f$ is integrated on $[0,1]^3$. Choosing $\sigma=r$ and $\tau=r+t$ gives the paper’s heat-shift identity at period one. Fourier integrals are assigned zero when nonintegrable. This theorem does not state the lemma’s norm estimates or its continuity clause.
pdf-item-theorem-3-7.Breakdown.Periodic.SourceCont.Internal.f: For any fixed field $f$, `Breakdown.Periodic.SourceCont.Internal.forceV_continuousOn` proves that the field with coefficients $e^{-4\pi^2\tau|n|^2}\mathbb P_n\hat f(n)$ varies continuously for $\tau>0$ in this norm. The coefficients are integrated on $[0,1]^3$ and assigned zero if nonintegrable. $\mathbb P_0=I$. For integrable fields this is projected heat flow. The paper uses mean-zero homogeneous spaces at every period. This theorem does not state the norm estimates or mean-zero advective forcing assertion.
pdf-item-theorem-3-7.Breakdown.Periodic.kernelSharpBound_hold: Equation (3.20) uses homogeneous mean-zero norms and quantifies over every $L>0$ and every $\tau>0$. `Breakdown.Periodic.kernelSharpBound_holds` proves the bilinear estimate only on the described unit-torus space and lag range. The lemma’s separate assertion that the advective forcing lies in $L^{3/2}$ and has mean zero is not supplied by these links.

ns-3late-periodic-force-bound.Breakdown.Periodic.ShellTorus.Internal.s: `Breakdown.Periodic.ShellTorus.Internal.sourceOp_threeHalves` gives $\|e^{\mu\tau\Delta}\mathbb P f_\mu\|_{H^1(\mathbb T^3)}\le C\mu^{1/4}\tau^{-3/4}\|A\|_{3/2}$ with one $C$. Compact support makes this $L^{3/2}$ norm finite. Equation (3.19) allows all mean-zero $L^{3/2}$ forces, all periods and all positive times. It uses the homogeneous norm.

ns-3late-periodic-force-shift.Breakdown.Periodic.Forced.Internal.force: For any field $f:\mathbb R^3\to\mathbb R^3$ and $0<\sigma\le\tau$, `Breakdown.Periodic.Forced.Internal.forceV_eq_heat` gives $F(\tau)=G(\tau-\sigma)F(\sigma)$, where $\widehat{F(r)}(n)=e^{-4\pi^2r|n|^2}\mathbb P_n\hat f(n)$ for $r>0$ and $\hat f$ is integrated on $[0,1]^3$. Choosing $\sigma=r$ and $\tau=r+t$ gives the paper’s heat-shift identity at period one. Fourier integrals are assigned zero when nonintegrable. This link supplies the shift identity. Continuity is a separate conclusion.
ns-3late-periodic-force-shift.Breakdown.Periodic.SourceCont.Internal.f: For any fixed field $f$, `Breakdown.Periodic.SourceCont.Internal.forceV_continuousOn` proves that the field with coefficients $e^{-4\pi^2\tau|n|^2}\mathbb P_n\hat f(n)$ varies continuously for $\tau>0$ in this norm. The coefficients are integrated on $[0,1]^3$ and assigned zero if nonintegrable. $\mathbb P_0=I$. For integrable fields this is projected heat flow. The paper uses mean-zero homogeneous spaces at every period. The passage uses this continuity.

ns-3late-periodic-kernel-bound.Breakdown.Periodic.KernelSharpBound: The formal periodic space consists of real solenoidal fields of period one with norm $\|u\|_{H^1}^2=\sum_{n\in\mathbb Z^3}(1+4\pi^2|n|^2)|\hat u(n)|^2$. The mean may be nonzero. One $C>0$ gives $\|K_{\mathbb T}(\tau)(u,v)\|_{H^1}\le C\tau^{-3/4}\|u\|_{H^1}\|v\|_{H^1}$ for every $u,v$ and $0<\tau\le1$. Equation (3.20) uses homogeneous mean-zero norms and quantifies over every $L>0$ and every $\tau>0$. `Breakdown.Periodic.KernelSharpBound` states the short-time bound.
ns-3late-periodic-kernel-bound.Breakdown.Periodic.kernelSharpBound_hold: The formal periodic space consists of real solenoidal fields of period one with norm $\|u\|_{H^1}^2=\sum_{n\in\mathbb Z^3}(1+4\pi^2|n|^2)|\hat u(n)|^2$. The mean may be nonzero. One $C>0$ gives $\|K_{\mathbb T}(\tau)(u,v)\|_{H^1}\le C\tau^{-3/4}\|u\|_{H^1}\|v\|_{H^1}$ for every $u,v$ and $0<\tau\le1$. Equation (3.20) uses homogeneous mean-zero norms and quantifies over every $L>0$ and every $\tau>0$. `Breakdown.Periodic.kernelSharpBound_holds` proves the short-time bound.

ns-3late-periodic-abstract-realization.Breakdown.Periodic.stepFrame: For $0<\mu\le1$, the formal construction sets $G_\mu(t)=G(\mu t)$ and $K_\mu(\tau)=\mu^{3/4}K_{\mathbb T}(\mu\tau)$, and supplies the heat, symmetry, continuity and shift laws and $\|K_\mu(\tau)\|\le C\tau^{-3/4}$ for $0<\tau\le1$, with the same $C$. The paper instead gives the full positive-time assumptions on homogeneous mean-zero spaces for every spatial period. The formal construction rescales operators on one fixed space.

pdf-item-equation-3-21.Breakdown.Periodic.TransplantNorm: `Breakdown.Periodic.TransplantNorm` states that the squared inhomogeneous norm after multiplying this field by $\mu^{1/4}$ equals $\|\nabla g\|_2^2+\mu\|g\|_2^2$. Equation (3.21) instead relates homogeneous norms of an arbitrary periodic field on two different tori. The same numbered equation also states heat and bilinear covariance between periods. It contains neither.
pdf-item-equation-3-21.Breakdown.Periodic.stepFrame: For $0<\mu\le1$, the formal construction sets $G_\mu(t)=G(\mu t)$ and $K_\mu(\tau)=\mu^{3/4}K_{\mathbb T}(\mu\tau)$, and supplies the heat, symmetry, continuity and shift laws and $\|K_\mu(\tau)\|\le C\tau^{-3/4}$ for $0<\tau\le1$, with the same $C$. Equation (3.21) instead uses spatial dilation between tori of periods $L$ and $L/\sqrt\mu$ and the homogeneous norm. The construction contains no such spatial map or inter-period covariance identity.

adapted.N2-10.1.Breakdown.Spectral.exists_dichotomy: `Breakdown.Spectral.exists_dichotomy` constructs a finite-rank real projection commuting with the period map, under the compact-perturbation and small-norm assumptions. Its two power bounds separate the finitely many directions that must be corrected from the faster-decaying complement.

adapted.N2-11.1.Breakdown.PeriodicSimilarityProfileExist: `Breakdown.PeriodicSimilarityProfileExists` includes a positive period $S$ and orthogonal recurrence as hypotheses for the profile reduction. The period is part of the existence assertion and need not be the least one.

ns-s4-003.Breakdown.physicalField: For $t<1$, set $u_{s_0}(t,x)=(1-t)^{-1/2}W(s_0-\log(1-t),x/\sqrt{1-t})$. The definition fixes terminal time one and allows every real phase $s_0$. The paper allows any $T>0$ and uses $s=\log(T/(T-t))$. The formulas agree at $T=1,s_0=0$. Their relation for other $T$ is the parabolic rescaling $u_T^*(t,x)=T^{-1/2}u_1^*(t/T,x/\sqrt T)$.

ns-s4-004.Breakdown.IsSimilarityProfile: `Breakdown.IsSimilarityProfile` requires a smooth velocity and pressure satisfying the similarity equations, with uniform operator-norm decay through two spatial velocity derivatives and decay of the pressure gradient. The bounds in (1.3) refer to the first two velocity orders.
ns-s4-004.Breakdown.PhysicalMomentum: Derivative norms in these hypotheses are operator norms. The paper states (1.3) for orders zero and one with the Euclidean norm of the coordinate derivatives. Remark 1.2 discusses the second derivative, and the displayed pressure-gradient hypothesis is an additional formal requirement. For $t<1$, set $u_{s_0}(t,x)=(1-t)^{-1/2}W(s_0-\log(1-t),x/\sqrt{1-t})$. With $p_{s_0}(t,x)=(1-t)^{-1}q(s_0-\log(1-t),x/\sqrt{1-t})$, `Breakdown.PhysicalMomentum` states $\partial_tu_{s_0}=\Delta u_{s_0}-(u_{s_0}\cdot\nabla)u_{s_0}-\nabla p_{s_0}$ at each $t<1,x\in\mathbb R^3$. The quoted phrase concerns joint smoothness and incompressibility. Those are not this assertion's conclusion.

pdf-item-equation-4-1.Breakdown.physicalField: For $t<1$, set $u_{s_0}(t,x)=(1-t)^{-1/2}W(s_0-\log(1-t),x/\sqrt{1-t})$. `Breakdown.physicalField` contains no inequality. From the order-zero profile bound $|W(s,y)|\le C/(1+|y|)$ one obtains $|u_{s_0}(t,x)|\le C/(\sqrt{1-t}+|x|)$ for $t<1$. The corresponding gradient calculation additionally uses the derivative bound and its norm convention. These estimates are absent from it.
pdf-item-equation-4-1.Breakdown.IsSimilarityProfile: For $u^*(t,x)=(1-t)^{-1/2}W(-\log(1-t),x/\sqrt{1-t})$, scaling gives the first bounds in (4.1), with the operator norm for $\nabla u^*$. The paper's Frobenius gradient norm can be up to $\sqrt3$ times that operator norm. The further comparison with $C/|x|$ or $C/|x|^2$ requires $x\ne0$ when using real division, since division by zero is assigned zero. The formal profile condition is a premise, not a proof of (4.1).
pdf-item-equation-4-1.Breakdown.embeddedProfileOrbit_holds: In a realization preserving the homogeneous $H^1$ norm, rotations and dilations and taking the specified weak solutions to mild solutions, the theorem produces the continuous curve $w(s)$ represented by $W(s,\cdot)$. It is nonzero somewhere, satisfies $w(s+S)=\rho_Rw(s)$ and the similarity-time Duhamel equation. Proposition 4.1 instead states the corresponding properties for the physical curve on $[0,1)$. The change of time variable is a separate step.
pdf-item-equation-4-1.Breakdown.physicalMild_unconditional: Assume the represented profile slices are continuous in the homogeneous $H^1$ norm and that the realization sends weak solutions with continuous square-integrable time differences to mild solutions. For every real $s_0$ and $0<T<1$, `Breakdown.physicalMild_unconditional` proves that $u_{s_0}$ is continuous and satisfies the Duhamel equation on $[0,T]$, with an integrable nonlinear term. It supplies neither the recurrence nor the nonvanishing in Proposition 4.1. Its profile assumptions also include the extra decay just stated.

ns-s4-007.Breakdown.embeddedProfileOrbit_holds: In a realization preserving the homogeneous $H^1$ norm, rotations and dilations and taking the specified weak solutions to mild solutions, the theorem produces the continuous curve $w(s)$ represented by $W(s,\cdot)$. It is nonzero somewhere, satisfies $w(s+S)=\rho_Rw(s)$ and the similarity-time Duhamel equation. Proposition 4.1 instead states the corresponding properties for the physical curve on $[0,1)$. The change of time variable is a separate step.
ns-s4-007.Breakdown.physicalMild_unconditional: Assume the represented profile slices are continuous in the homogeneous $H^1$ norm and that the realization sends weak solutions with continuous square-integrable time differences to mild solutions. For every real $s_0$ and $0<T<1$, `Breakdown.physicalMild_unconditional` proves that $u_{s_0}$ is continuous and satisfies the Duhamel equation on $[0,T]$, with an integrable nonlinear term. It supplies neither the recurrence nor the nonvanishing in Proposition 4.1. Its profile assumptions also include the extra decay just stated.

pdf-item-equation-4-2.Breakdown.MildFramework.IsOrbit: The recurrence component of `Breakdown.MildFramework.IsOrbit` is $w(s+S)=\rho_Rw(s)$ for all real $s$. For $\lambda=e^{-S}$, the paper's physical identity follows by the logarithmic change of time together with $D_\mu D_\eta=D_{\mu\eta}$ and commutation of $\rho_R$ with the dilations. That identity is not written in this condition.
pdf-item-equation-4-2.Breakdown.MildFramework.selfSimilar: On $t<1$ its scale is positive. `Breakdown.MildFramework.selfSimilar` requires no recurrence, continuity or equation. In the paper $D_\mu f(x)=\sqrt\mu f(\sqrt\mu x)$. For $s_0=0$, $S>0$ and $\lambda=e^{-S}$, the paper's recurrence additionally needs $w(s+S)=\rho_Rw(s)$, commutation of $\rho_R$ with $D_\mu$ and the dilation composition law. The definition alone imposes none of those recurrence hypotheses.
pdf-item-equation-4-2.Breakdown.ProfilePieceStatement: `Breakdown.ProfilePieceStatement` states that $a_n$ is a continuous mild solution on $[0,L]$, $D_\mu a_n(L)=a_{n+1}(0)$ and $a_{n+k}=\rho a_n$. If $\|w(s)\|\le M$ for every real $s$, it also states $\|a_n\|_\infty\le e^{S/(4k)}M$. The paper's formula instead holds on a whole period for every $0\le\sigma<1$, $u^*(1-\lambda^n+\lambda^n\sigma)=\rho_R^nD_{\lambda^{-n}}u^*(\sigma)$, $\lambda=e^{-S}$. It states matching and a one-period shift for the short pieces, without that whole-period identity as a conclusion.
pdf-item-equation-4-2.Breakdown.orbitBound: `Breakdown.orbitBound` gives one uniform upper norm bound for the continuous recurrent orbit by the isometry and compactness of a period interval. Equation (4.2) uses this recurrence at the level of the physical velocity after dilation.
pdf-item-equation-4-2.Breakdown.orbitNorm: Let $\rho$ be a surjective linear isometry commuting with $G,K,D$, including their assigned values at all real parameters. Let $S>0$ and let $w:\mathbb R\to X$ be continuous and nonzero somewhere, with $w(s+S)=\rho w(s)$. For $a\le s$, require the Bochner integral to exist and $w(s)=D_{e^{-(s-a)}}G(1-e^{-(s-a)})w(a)+\int_a^sD_{e^{-(s-r)}}K(1-e^{-(s-r)})(w(r),w(r))\,dr$. `Breakdown.orbitNorm` supplies $c>0$ with $\|w(s)\|\ge c$ for every real $s$. Dilation gives $\|u^*(t)\|\ge c(1-t)^{-1/4}$ for $u^*(t)=D_{(1-t)^{-1}}w(-\log(1-t))$, $0\le t<1$. The uniform upper bound and hence the complete two-sided assertion (4.4) are separate.
pdf-item-equation-4-2.Breakdown.Freq.DilationAlgebra: `Breakdown.Freq.DilationAlgebra` asserts, for $\mu,\eta>0$, $\|D_\mu x\|_X=\mu^{1/4}\|x\|_X$, $D_1=I$, $D_\mu D_\eta=D_{\mu\eta}$, $D_\mu G(\mu t)=G(t)D_\mu$ for $t\ge0$, and that $D_\mu$ is given by this frequency formula. At $\mu=(1-t)^{-1}$, $t<1$, this gives the factor $(1-t)^{-1/4}$. For $u^*(t)=D_{(1-t)^{-1}}w(-\log(1-t))$, the two-sided estimate (4.4) also needs positive lower and finite upper bounds for $\|w(s)\|$. Neither orbit bound is part of this formal assertion.

ns-s4-016.Breakdown.physicalTime: For $t<1$ and $\lambda=e^{-S}$, the formal logarithmic change of variables increases by $S$ at the displayed time.

ns-s4-017.Breakdown.MildFramework.gluePieces: Outside each interval a curve is extended by its endpoint value. The formal construction generally takes $\mu=e^{-S/k}$, so one similarity period contains $k$ short intervals. The paper's times $t_n=1-\lambda^n$, $\lambda=e^{-S}$, are whole-period endpoints. They correspond to $k=1$, or to every kth short endpoint. Neither recurrence nor a norm rate is a conclusion of the reconstruction definition.

ns-s4-018.Breakdown.ProfilePieceStatement: `Breakdown.ProfilePieceStatement` states that $a_n$ is a continuous mild solution on $[0,L]$, $D_\mu a_n(L)=a_{n+1}(0)$ and $a_{n+k}=\rho a_n$. If $\|w(s)\|\le M$ for every real $s$, it also states $\|a_n\|_\infty\le e^{S/(4k)}M$. The paper's formula instead holds on a whole period for every $0\le\sigma<1$, $u^*(1-\lambda^n+\lambda^n\sigma)=\rho_R^nD_{\lambda^{-n}}u^*(\sigma)$, $\lambda=e^{-S}$. It states matching and a one-period shift for the short pieces, without that whole-period identity as a conclusion.
ns-s4-018.Breakdown.MildFramework.selfSimilar: On $t<1$ its scale is positive. `Breakdown.MildFramework.selfSimilar` requires no recurrence, continuity or equation. In the physical realization $D_\mu f(x)=\sqrt\mu f(\sqrt\mu x)$. For natural $n$, the factor $\rho_R^n$ in the paper's identity requires iteration of the separate relation $w(s+S)=\rho_Rw(s)$. It neither assumes nor proves that relation, and it asserts no whole-period identity by itself.
ns-s4-018.Breakdown.stepData: The physical datum correction is $Je\in J(V)$. Its bound also uses $\|J\|$. The paper's correction space is represented by $J(V)$ when $C$ consists of smooth compactly supported solenoidal fields. `Breakdown.stepData` controls the bounded sequence norm and the coordinate $e$. It does not state the map $C_\kappa\to E\times C_\kappa$ of Proposition 4.3.
ns-s4-018.Breakdown.exists_section: `Breakdown.exists_section` gives a bounded lift of the finite-dimensional range of a projection through a chosen dense linear subspace. The lift is used with the period decomposition of Lemma 4.2 when choosing the test-field correction.

ns-s4-019.Breakdown.orbitBound: `Breakdown.orbitBound` gives a uniform upper bound on the continuous recurrent orbit. In the physical variable it becomes the upper $(1-t)^{-1/4}$ estimate by the $\dot H^1$ dilation law. The positive lower bound uses nonvanishing and a separate result.
ns-s4-019.Breakdown.orbitNorm: Let $\rho$ be a surjective linear isometry commuting with $G,K,D$, including their assigned values at all real parameters. Let $S>0$ and let $w:\mathbb R\to X$ be continuous and nonzero somewhere, with $w(s+S)=\rho w(s)$. For $a\le s$, require the Bochner integral to exist and $w(s)=D_{e^{-(s-a)}}G(1-e^{-(s-a)})w(a)+\int_a^sD_{e^{-(s-r)}}K(1-e^{-(s-r)})(w(r),w(r))\,dr$. `Breakdown.orbitNorm` supplies $c>0$ with $\|w(s)\|\ge c$ for every real $s$. ns-s4-060.Breakdown.Freq.DilationAlgebra: For $\mu,\eta>0$ `Breakdown.Freq.DilationAlgebra` states $\|D_\mu x\|=\mu^{1/4}\|x\|$, $D_1=I$, $D_\mu D_\eta=D_{\mu\eta}$, $D_\mu G(\mu t)=G(t)D_\mu$ for $t\ge0$, and agreement of $D_\mu$ with the dilation on $L^2$. For natural $n$, $\lambda=e^{-S}>0$ and $\sigma\ge0$, set $\mu=\lambda^n$ and $t=\sigma$ to obtain $D_{\lambda^n}G(\lambda^n\sigma)=G(\sigma)D_{\lambda^n}$. Commutation with $\rho_R$ and the identification of the rescaled initial vector are additional steps in the paper's equation. They are not components of this dilation assertion.

ns-s4-061.Breakdown.MildFramework.stepOp: `Breakdown.MildFramework.stepOp` defines the linearized interaction on a rescaled interval by integrating $2K(t-r)(a_n(r),v(r))$, where $a_n$ is the reference piece. Applying the kernel-scaling identity identifies it with the period operator in the paper.

ns-s4-062.Breakdown.stepMap: An operator without a bounded inverse is assigned inverse zero. If $I-A_n$ is invertible, $(I-A_n)^{-1}\Gamma x$ solves the linear interval equation, and $S_nx$ is its rescaled endpoint. In the application $Y=C([0,L];X)$, $\Gamma x(t)=G(t)x$, and $Ev=D_\mu v(L)$. When $I-A_n$ is invertible, the corresponding interval trajectory with a source is $(I-A_n)^{-1}(\Gamma\chi+g)$. `Breakdown.stepMap` here applies $E$ only to the homogeneous trajectory $(I-A_n)^{-1}\Gamma\chi$. It states neither the inhomogeneous trajectory identity nor the paper's unsplit decomposition on $[0,1-e^{-S}]$.

ns-s4-063.Breakdown.orbitSeq: At $\theta=0$ division is assigned zero. The dichotomy arguments impose $\theta>0$. For $\theta>0$, set $\chi_n=\theta^nx_n$ and $f_n=\theta^nc_n$ to obtain the unweighted recurrence. The paper also gives a specific endpoint expression for $f_n$ using the full-period solution operator $\mathcal U$. `Breakdown.orbitSeq` begins with a supplied sequence $c_n$ and contains no such endpoint formula.

adapted.N2-21.1.Breakdown.exists_section: For a finite-rank bounded projection, `Breakdown.exists_section` lifts each range basis vector through any dense linear subspace. With the dense class of test fields, the lifted vectors are smooth, compactly supported and solenoidal.

ns-s4-069.Breakdown.DiscreteDichotomyInternal.step: `Breakdown.DiscreteDichotomyInternal.step_tailSum` proves $\Theta^{-1}(MU(c)+Pc_0)=U((c_{j+1})_{j\ge0})$. Iterating and restoring the normalization $f_j=\Theta^jc_j$ gives the future-tail form in the paper. This theorem does not identify $c_j$ with the source derived from a global solution, and it does not supply the complementary finite sum.
ns-s4-069.Breakdown.DiscreteDichotomyInternal.rec_: `Breakdown.DiscreteDichotomyInternal.rec_formula` proves $w_n=B^nw_0+\sum_{m<n}B^{n-1-m}d_m$. At $n=0$ the sum is empty, for $m<n$ the exponent $n-1-m$ is a nonnegative integer. Apply this with $w_n=(I-P_{\mathrm u})\chi_n$, $B=\mathcal M$ and $d_n=(I-P_{\mathrm u})f_n$, using commutation, to obtain the second identity. No infinite-series identity is concluded.

ns-s4-070.Breakdown.DiscreteDichotomyStatement: `Breakdown.DiscreteDichotomyStatement` supplies a bounded linear $U:\ell^\infty(X)\to X$ with $PUc=Uc$ and a constant $K\prime$. If $Px_0=Uc$, the normalized recurrence $x_{n+1}=\Theta^{-1}(Mx_n+c_n)$ satisfies $\|x_n\|\le K\prime(\|x_0\|+\|c\|_\infty)$ for all $n$. Finite rank of $P$ is not assumed here. For $\chi_n=\Theta^nx_n$ and $f_n=\Theta^nc_n$, the uniform formal bound becomes geometric decay in $n$. The paper derives that decay from the two series in (4.11). It instead assumes forward and inverse geometric bounds at the two radii and works directly with a bounded normalized source sequence.

ns-s4-071.Breakdown.PeriodicInverseStatement: `Breakdown.PeriodicInverseStatement` supplies a bounded linear $\mathcal R:\ell^\infty(Y)\to X\times\ell^\infty(Y)$. For $(e,z)=\mathcal Rg$, it requires $e\in\operatorname{ran}P$, $z_0-A_0z_0-\Gamma Je=g_0$ and $z_n-A_nz_n-\theta^{-1}\Gamma Ez_{n-1}=g_n$ for $n\ge1$. The product norm is $\max(\|e\|,\sup_n\|z_n\|_Y)$. When $Y=C([0,L];X)$, boundedness of $\mathcal R$ controls $\sup_n\|z_n\|_Y$. Restoring a factor $\theta^n$ gives decay for short-interval corrections. The paper estimates whole-period curves by $\Theta^n\|g\|_\kappa$ using its full-period solution operator. That global source norm and the whole-period estimate are not named in it.

ns-s4-072.Breakdown.MildFramework.gluePieces: Outside each interval a curve is extended by its endpoint value. If the dilation law is $\|D_\eta x\|=\eta^{1/4}\|x\|$ for $\eta>0$, then $\|v(t)\|=\mu^{-n/4}\|a_n(\sigma)\|$. A separate bound $\|a_n\|\lesssim\theta^n$ and a choice $\theta=\mu^\kappa$ give the type of weighted rate used in the paper. The reconstruction definition supplies no such sequence estimate or bound in the global $C_\kappa$ norm.

ns-s4-073.Breakdown.StepDataStatement: The physical datum correction is $Je\in J(V)$. Its bound also uses $\|J\|$. The map $\mathcal R$ is bounded and linear on interval sequences. The paper concludes boundedness and linearity of a map into a global curve space with norm $\sup_{t<1}(1-t)^{1/4-\kappa}\|v(t)\|$. That curve must be reconstructed and its weighted estimate proved. Neither is a stated conclusion of this sequence assertion.
ns-s4-073.Breakdown.PeriodicInverseStatement: `Breakdown.PeriodicInverseStatement` supplies a bounded linear $\mathcal R:\ell^\infty(Y)\to X\times\ell^\infty(Y)$. For $(e,z)=\mathcal Rg$, it requires $e\in\operatorname{ran}P$, $z_0-A_0z_0-\Gamma Je=g_0$ and $z_n-A_nz_n-\theta^{-1}\Gamma Ez_{n-1}=g_n$ for $n\ge1$. The product norm is $\max(\|e\|,\sup_n\|z_n\|_Y)$. Linearity is explicit in it, but its domain and codomain are spaces of bounded sequences. The paper's global operator additionally uses the dependence of its source sequence on a global curve and the joining of rescaled interval solutions. Those maps and their global weighted norm do not appear in it.

ns-s4-074.Breakdown.HeatBilinear: The kernel bound is assumed only for $0<\tau\le1$, while (3.12) assumes it for all $\tau>0$. The paper's abstract setting assumes $X$ is Banach. Completeness is not part of this formal data definition. It is imposed in the integral and correction statements. `Breakdown.HeatBilinear` supplies the common operator assumptions, without itself proving either nonlinear lemma.

ns-s4-075.Breakdown.Periodic.SeqPerturbation: If $\xi\in X$ obeys $64\|\mathcal R\|^2C_KL^{1/4}(\rho+\|\xi\|)\le1$, `Breakdown.Periodic.SeqPerturbation` supplies $e$ and $z_n$ with $\max(\|e\|,\sup_n\|z_n\|_Y)\le2\|\mathcal R\|(\rho+\|\xi\|)$. The curves $v_n=a_n+\theta^nz_n$ are exact mild solutions on $[0,L]$, $v_{n+1}(0)=c\,v_n(L)$ and $z_0(0)=\xi+Je$. The paper's (4.16) defines one global residual $F^{\mathrm a}$ and one global linear map $\mathcal L$. It uses the residuals $r_n$ and coupled linear equations on a sequence of compact intervals, with an endpoint term after the first interval. It is a conditional correction assertion, not a definition of the two global expressions.

ns-s4-076.Breakdown.Periodic.SeqPerturbation: If $\xi\in X$ obeys $64\|\mathcal R\|^2C_KL^{1/4}(\rho+\|\xi\|)\le1$, `Breakdown.Periodic.SeqPerturbation` supplies $e$ and $z_n$ with $\max(\|e\|,\sup_n\|z_n\|_Y)\le2\|\mathcal R\|(\rho+\|\xi\|)$. The curves $v_n=a_n+\theta^nz_n$ are exact mild solutions on $[0,L]$, $v_{n+1}(0)=c\,v_n(L)$ and $z_0(0)=\xi+Je$. The residual hypothesis is $a_n=\Gamma_na_n(0)+B_n(a_n,a_n)+r_n$. If $r_n=0$, this is precisely the mild identity on that closed interval. Continuity and integrability follow from the interval setting. The paper states an equivalence for a single curve on $[0,1)$. This linked assertion does not state that global equivalence.

ns-s4-077.Breakdown.PiecePerturbationStatement: If $a(t)=G(t)a(0)+B_T(a,a)(t)$ and $v(t)=G(t)x+2B_T(a,v)(t)+B_T(v,v)(t)$, `Breakdown.PiecePerturbationStatement` concludes $v(0)=x$ and $a+v$ is a continuous mild solution on $[0,T]$, including integrability of its Duhamel term. It uses an exact background $a$ and the implication from its perturbation identity to a mild solution. The paper displays an algebraic identity valid for an arbitrary approximate background and an independent datum displacement. The residual term of that identity is absent from the formal perturbation statement.

ns-s4-078.Breakdown.Periodic.SeqPerturbation: If $\xi\in X$ obeys $64\|\mathcal R\|^2C_KL^{1/4}(\rho+\|\xi\|)\le1$, `Breakdown.Periodic.SeqPerturbation` supplies $e$ and $z_n$ with $\max(\|e\|,\sup_n\|z_n\|_Y)\le2\|\mathcal R\|(\rho+\|\xi\|)$. The curves $v_n=a_n+\theta^nz_n$ are exact mild solutions on $[0,L]$, $v_{n+1}(0)=c\,v_n(L)$ and $z_0(0)=\xi+Je$. The paper's (4.17) is an equivalence obtained by bilinear expansion before any smallness or inverse hypothesis is imposed. It specifies the construction of exact interval solutions under the inverse, matching and smallness conditions stated here. It does not state that unrestricted global algebraic equivalence.

ns-s4-080.Breakdown.ContractionInternal.exists_sma: `Breakdown.ContractionInternal.exists_small_fixed` assumes $\|\Phi(z)\|\le b+K\|z\|^2$ for every $z$ and $\|\Phi(z)-\Phi(w)\|\le K(\|z\|+\|w\|)\|z-w\|$ for every $z,w$. It proves that some $z$ satisfies $\Phi(z)=z$ and $\|z\|\le2b$. To use this theorem in the paper, $Z$ must be its complete weighted curve space and $\Phi$ the second component of the right-inverse image of the quadratic expression. Establishing the weighted Duhamel bounds is a separate step. They are not proved by this fixed-point theorem.

ns-s4-081.Breakdown.varConstIntegral: For $a\le b$ and continuous $f,g:[a,b]\to X$ with $\|f(s)\|\le M$, $\|g(s)\|\le N$, `Breakdown.varConstIntegral` proves that $B(f,g)(t)=\int_a^tK(t-r)(f(r),g(r))\,dr$ exists and is continuous on $[a,b]$. If $t-a\le1$, then $\|B(f,g)(t)\|\le4C_K(t-a)^{1/4}MN$. It uses constant bounds $M,N$ on a compact interval. Equation (4.18) instead integrates the singular factor against the time weight $(1-t\prime)^{\kappa-1/2}$ and identifies a constant by an integral over $(0,\infty)$. Neither that substitution nor that weighted estimate is stated by it.

ns-s4-083.Breakdown.varConstIntegral: For $a\le b$ and continuous $f,g:[a,b]\to X$ with $\|f(s)\|\le M$, $\|g(s)\|\le N$, `Breakdown.varConstIntegral` proves that $B(f,g)(t)=\int_a^tK(t-r)(f(r),g(r))\,dr$ exists and is continuous on $[a,b]$. If $t-a\le1$, then $\|B(f,g)(t)\|\le4C_K(t-a)^{1/4}MN$. For continuous curves on $[0,1)$, each restriction to $[0,b]$, $b<1$, is bounded, so it gives the continuity part of Lemma 4.7. The lemma also asserts a single constant depending only on $\kappa,C_K$ for its global weighted estimates. It has no global weighted norm or such constant.
ns-s4-083.Breakdown.PieceOperatorStatement: For $T>0$, `Breakdown.PieceOperatorStatement` specifies $B_T(f,g)(t)=\int_0^tK(t-r)(f(r),g(r))\,dr$ and $\Gamma_Tx(t)=G(t)x$ on $C([0,T];X)$, with $\|\Gamma_T\|\le1$ and $\|B_T\|\le4C_KT^{1/4}$ when $T\le1$. All curve norms here are unweighted supremum norms. The paper's Lemma 4.7 concerns global norms on $[0,1)$ and includes a mixed estimate with one input in $C_0$. It concerns the unweighted supremum norm on $[0,T]$, with the explicit factor $4C_KT^{1/4}$. It does not assert those global estimates or their common $\kappa$-dependent constant.

pdf-item-equation-4-19.Breakdown.PieceOperatorStatement: For $T>0$, `Breakdown.PieceOperatorStatement` specifies $B_T(f,g)(t)=\int_0^tK(t-r)(f(r),g(r))\,dr$ and $\Gamma_Tx(t)=G(t)x$ on $C([0,T];X)$, with $\|\Gamma_T\|\le1$ and $\|B_T\|\le4C_KT^{1/4}$ when $T\le1$. All curve norms here are unweighted supremum norms. The paper's (4.19) uses $\|v\|_\kappa=\sup_{0\le t<1}(1-t)^{1/4-\kappa}\|v(t)\|$ for $0<\kappa<1/4$. It has no such weight or half-open-time domain. Its compact-interval bound is not the displayed global bilinear estimate.

pdf-item-equation-4-20.Breakdown.HeatBilinear: `Breakdown.HeatBilinear` assumes the heat operators are contractions for all nonnegative times. Multiplying their norm bound by $(1-t)^{1/4-\kappa}\le1$ on $[0,1)$ for $0<\kappa<1/4$ gives the estimate in (4.20).

ns-s4-086.Breakdown.varConstIntegral: For $a\le b$ and continuous $f,g:[a,b]\to X$ with $\|f(s)\|\le M$, $\|g(s)\|\le N$, `Breakdown.varConstIntegral` proves that $B(f,g)(t)=\int_a^tK(t-r)(f(r),g(r))\,dr$ exists and is continuous on $[a,b]$. If $t-a\le1$, then $\|B(f,g)(t)\|\le4C_K(t-a)^{1/4}MN$. Equation (4.21) instead assumes $f$ bounded on $[0,1)$ and $g$ controlled by $\|g\|_0=\sup_{t<1}(1-t)^{1/4}\|g(t)\|$, and concludes a global $C_\kappa$ estimate. A constant bound for $g$ on a compact interval depends on its right endpoint and does not by itself state that global estimate. No exact counterpart of (4.21) occurs in the linked formal statement.

ns-s4-087.Breakdown.varConstIntegral: For $a\le b$ and continuous $f,g:[a,b]\to X$ with $\|f(s)\|\le M$, $\|g(s)\|\le N$, `Breakdown.varConstIntegral` proves that $B(f,g)(t)=\int_a^tK(t-r)(f(r),g(r))\,dr$ exists and is continuous on $[a,b]$. If $t-a\le1$, then $\|B(f,g)(t)\|\le4C_K(t-a)^{1/4}MN$. Each continuous input curve on $[0,1)$ is bounded on every $[0,b]$ with $b<1$. Applying this formal continuity conclusion to those restrictions proves continuity at every time before one, exactly the compact-interval argument in the paper. No weighted norm estimate is needed for this continuity component.

ns-s4-088.Breakdown.HeatBilinear: For a real normed space $X$, the formal kernel data include symmetric bounded bilinear $K(\tau)$ with $\|K(\tau)\|\le C_K\tau^{-3/4}$ for $0<\tau\le1$. Taking $\tau=t-t'$ for $0\le t'<t<1$ gives the first inequality in the paper's sentence. The subsequent estimates use the separate global definitions $\|v\|_\kappa=\sup_{s<1}(1-s)^{1/4-\kappa}\|v(s)\|$ and $\|g\|_0=\sup_{s<1}(1-s)^{1/4}\|g(s)\|$. Those norms and estimates are not part of the formal kernel data.

ns-s4-089.Breakdown.PieceOperatorStatement: For $T>0$, `Breakdown.PieceOperatorStatement` specifies $B_T(f,g)(t)=\int_0^tK(t-r)(f(r),g(r))\,dr$ and $\Gamma_Tx(t)=G(t)x$ on $C([0,T];X)$, with $\|\Gamma_T\|\le1$ and $\|B_T\|\le4C_KT^{1/4}$ when $T\le1$. All curve norms here are unweighted supremum norms. The explicit constant in the formal compact-interval bound is $4C_KT^{1/4}$. The paper compares the powers $2\kappa-1/2$ and $-1/4$ with $\kappa-1/2$ on $0<1-t'\le1$, then uses the integral in (4.18). Those exponent comparisons, that improper-integral constant and the resulting global weighted bounds are absent from it.
ns-s4-089.Breakdown.HeatBilinear: The formal heat-flow assumption on a real normed space is $\|G(t)\|\le1$ for every $t\ge0$, with $G(0)=I$ and strong continuity. For $0<\kappa<1/4$ and $\chi\in X$, multiplication by $(1-t)^{1/4-\kappa}\le1$ on $[0,1)$ yields $\sup_{t<1}(1-t)^{1/4-\kappa}\|G(t)\chi\|\le\|\chi\|$, which is the final assertion (4.20). The other weighted bilinear estimates in the quoted passage do not follow from this assumption alone.

ns-s4-090.Breakdown.Periodic.SeqPerturbation: If $\xi\in X$ obeys $64\|\mathcal R\|^2C_KL^{1/4}(\rho+\|\xi\|)\le1$, `Breakdown.Periodic.SeqPerturbation` supplies $e$ and $z_n$ with $\max(\|e\|,\sup_n\|z_n\|_Y)\le2\|\mathcal R\|(\rho+\|\xi\|)$. The curves $v_n=a_n+\theta^nz_n$ are exact mild solutions on $[0,L]$, $v_{n+1}(0)=c\,v_n(L)$ and $z_0(0)=\xi+Je$. It requires a normed complete correction space $E$ and a bounded inverse controlling both components. In Lemma 4.8, $E$ is only a vector space and the bound is imposed on the curve component alone. The formal source norm also separates residual and datum displacement. These differences prevent identification of this assertion with the full global lemma.
ns-s4-090.Breakdown.ContractionStatement: `Breakdown.ContractionStatement` concerns the nonlinear interval recurrence under a bounded right inverse and a small datum displacement. Lemma 4.8 also allows an independent residual and estimates a single global weighted curve, which is a further step.

pdf-item-equation-4-22.Breakdown.PeriodicInverseStatement: `Breakdown.PeriodicInverseStatement` supplies a bounded linear $\mathcal R:\ell^\infty(Y)\to X\times\ell^\infty(Y)$. For $(e,z)=\mathcal Rg$, it states $e\in\operatorname{ran}P$, $z_0-A_0z_0-\Gamma Je=g_0$ and $z_n-A_nz_n-\theta^{-1}\Gamma Ez_{n-1}=g_n$ for $n\ge1$. The product norm is $\max(\|e\|,\sup_n\|z_n\|_Y)$. The formal inverse acts on $\ell^\infty(Y)$ and controls the maximum of the initial-coordinate norm and the sequence norm. The paper's (4.22) assumes a right inverse on $C_\kappa([0,1);X)$ and bounds only its trajectory component. It also supplies an inverse from dichotomy hypotheses, whereas (4.22) is an inverse hypothesis for a nonlinear lemma.

ns-s4-092.Breakdown.Periodic.SeqPerturbation: The formal smallness condition uses the sum of a residual bound $\rho$ and the norm of the datum displacement $\xi$. Equation (4.23) instead uses $\|e^{t\Delta}\chi-F^{\mathrm a}\|_\kappa$, which may be smaller because it retains cancellation. The formal norm is that of bounded interval sequences and its right inverse controls both components. The paper uses a global weighted norm and a bound on the curve component.

ns-s4-093.Breakdown.Periodic.SeqPerturbation: If $\xi\in X$ obeys $64\|\mathcal R\|^2C_KL^{1/4}(\rho+\|\xi\|)\le1$, `Breakdown.Periodic.SeqPerturbation` supplies $e$ and $z_n$ with $\max(\|e\|,\sup_n\|z_n\|_Y)\le2\|\mathcal R\|(\rho+\|\xi\|)$. The curves $v_n=a_n+\theta^nz_n$ are exact mild solutions on $[0,L]$, $v_{n+1}(0)=c\,v_n(L)$ and $z_0(0)=\xi+Je$. It bounds the initial coordinate and every normalized interval correction by $2\|\mathcal R\|(\rho+\|\xi\|)$. Equation (4.24) bounds a single global correction by twice the norm of the combined forcing after the curve-component inverse bound. Joining the interval solutions and relating their norms to $C_\kappa$ require separate steps. The constants and norms should not be identified without them.

ns-s4-094.Breakdown.Periodic.SeqPerturbation: If $\xi\in X$ obeys $64\|\mathcal R\|^2C_KL^{1/4}(\rho+\|\xi\|)\le1$, `Breakdown.Periodic.SeqPerturbation` supplies $e$ and $z_n$ with $\max(\|e\|,\sup_n\|z_n\|_Y)\le2\|\mathcal R\|(\rho+\|\xi\|)$. The curves $v_n=a_n+\theta^nz_n$ are exact mild solutions on $[0,L]$, $v_{n+1}(0)=c\,v_n(L)$ and $z_0(0)=\xi+Je$. It gives exact mildness on each closed interval, matching endpoints, and the initial correction $\xi+Je$. The paper states one solution on $[0,1)$ with its datum. A joining argument and the physical rescaling are required to obtain that single curve from the interval conclusions.

ns-s4-095.Breakdown.ContractionInternal.exists_sma: `Breakdown.ContractionInternal.exists_small_fixed` assumes $\|\Phi(z)\|\le b+K\|z\|^2$ for every $z$ and $\|\Phi(z)-\Phi(w)\|\le K(\|z\|+\|w\|)\|z-w\|$ for every $z,w$. It proves that some $z$ satisfies $\Phi(z)=z$ and $\|z\|\le2b$. For the paper's application, take $b=C_{\mathcal R}\|e^{t\Delta}\chi-F^{\mathrm a}\|_\kappa$ and $K=CC_{\mathcal R}$ with nonnegative constants. If $C>0$ and $\varepsilon_1=(8C)^{-1}$, (4.23) implies $8Kb\le1$ and the ball radius is $\delta=2b$. The fixed-point theorem does not establish that the heat curve belongs to $C_\kappa$, or verify its two bounds for this particular $\Phi$.

ns-s4-096.Breakdown.ContractionInternal.exists_sma: `Breakdown.ContractionInternal.exists_small_fixed` assumes $\|\Phi(z)\|\le b+K\|z\|^2$ for every $z$ and $\|\Phi(z)-\Phi(w)\|\le K(\|z\|+\|w\|)\|z-w\|$ for every $z,w$. It proves that some $z$ satisfies $\Phi(z)=z$ and $\|z\|\le2b$. It accepts a globally defined map on a complete normed abelian group. The paper chooses $Z=C_\kappa([0,1);X)$ and $\Phi(v)$ as the curve component of $\mathcal R[e^{t\Delta}\chi-F^{\mathrm a}+\mathcal B(v,v)]$. That particular map, completeness of its weighted space and the two required estimates must be supplied before applying the theorem.

ns-s4-097.Breakdown.ContractionInternal.exists_sma: The assumed formal estimate $\|\Phi(z)\|\le b+K\|z\|^2$ gives this ball bound with radius $2b=\delta$ and $8Kb\le1$.

ns-s4-098.Breakdown.ContractionInternal.exists_sma: `Breakdown.ContractionInternal.exists_small_fixed` assumes $\|\Phi(z)\|\le b+K\|z\|^2$ for every $z$ and $\|\Phi(z)-\Phi(w)\|\le K(\|z\|+\|w\|)\|z-w\|$ for every $z,w$. It proves that some $z$ satisfies $\Phi(z)=z$ and $\|z\|\le2b$. For $\|z\|,\|w\|\le\delta=2b$, the assumed difference estimate gives Lipschitz constant at most $2K\delta=4Kb\le1/2$. The paper verifies the required difference estimate by expanding its bilinear Duhamel term and applying the right-inverse bound. That expansion and those operator bounds are hypotheses to be established for this application, rather than conclusions of the general theorem.

s1-outline-contraction.Breakdown.ContractionStatement: The application takes $Y=C([0,h];X)$, but `Breakdown.ContractionStatement` allows any real Banach space $Y$. The correspondence between the sequence solution and the continuous physical mild equation is an additional step.

ns5.cutoff.solenoidal.Breakdown.Periodic.cutoffDivergenceFree: `Breakdown.Periodic.cutoffDivergenceFree` assumes no support or size conditions on $\chi$ and therefore gives no support radius, no equality on an inner ball, and no norm bound. Its radial-potential premise is proved in the preceding curl theorem. For a smooth solenoidal field and a smooth scalar cutoff, it proves that the vector-potential cutoff is smooth and solenoidal. Take the centre to be zero and the scalar cutoff to be $\eta(x/r)$.

ns5.cutoff.scalar.Breakdown.Freq.Internal.NiceApprox.stdBu: The fixed formal bump has inner and outer radii $1,2$. Choosing $\eta(x)=b(2x)$ gives precisely the paper's radii $1/2,1$.

pdf-item-equation-5-1.Breakdown.Periodic.homotopyPotential: At centre zero and with $g=u^*(t)$, `Breakdown.Periodic.homotopyPotential` is exactly this integral. It asserts no curl or cutoff property.
pdf-item-equation-5-1.Breakdown.Periodic.cutoffField: `Breakdown.Periodic.cutoffField` is $\chi g+\nabla\chi\times A$. Identifying it with the displayed curl uses smoothness and the separate identity $\operatorname{curl}A=g$.
pdf-item-equation-5-1.Breakdown.Freq.Internal.NiceApprox.cutof: `Breakdown.Freq.Internal.NiceApprox.cutoff_isTestField` proves that the curl of a smooth potential multiplied by its fixed bump is a compact solenoidal field. Using the paper's cutoff requires $\eta(x)=b(2x)$ and $R=r/2$.

ns5.cutoff.parameter.Breakdown.Periodic.cutoffField: The cutoff radius enters through the chosen scalar function $\chi(x)=\eta(x/r)$. The formal formula has no independent radius parameter.

ns5.lemma5.1.geometry.Breakdown.Periodic.approxFieldProperties: `Breakdown.Periodic.approxFieldProperties_holds` proves smoothness for $t<T$ and support and agreement for the translated cutoff with radii $1/8,1/16$. The paper fixes terminal time one, centre zero and every radius $r>0$.
ns5.lemma5.1.geometry.Breakdown.Freq.Internal.NiceApprox.cutof: For a smooth potential and a nonzero radius `Breakdown.Freq.Internal.NiceApprox.cutoff_isTestField` gives membership in $C^\infty_{c,\mathrm{div}}$. It omits the asserted joint time smoothness, inner agreement and norm estimates.
ns5.lemma5.1.geometry.Breakdown.Periodic.cutoffGradientClose: `Breakdown.Periodic.cutoffGradientClose` gives qualitative convergence of the gradient of the rescaled cutoff to the reference gradient for a smooth similarity profile with the prescribed decay. Its cutoff is fixed in physical coordinates and the error becomes small as $T-t$ tends to zero. Lemma 5.1 displays an explicit rate in $r$.
ns5.lemma5.1.geometry.Breakdown.Periodic.cutoffMassBound: `Breakdown.Periodic.cutoffMassBound` is $\|f\|_2^2\le K/\sqrt{T-t}$ for the cutoff in similarity coordinates and $0<T-t\le1$. Taking square roots and setting $r=1/(8\sqrt{T-t})$ yields the stated growth only for this scaled family with $r\ge1/8$.

pdf-item-equation-5-2.Breakdown.Periodic.cutoffGradientClose: `Breakdown.Periodic.cutoffGradientClose` makes the squared gradient error in similarity coordinates at most any prescribed $\varepsilon>0$ once $T-t$ is small enough. It has no $r^{-1/2}$ rate or bound for every $r>0$. This linked statement addresses only the gradient estimate. The $L^2$ bound is the other assertion in the numbered display.
pdf-item-equation-5-2.Breakdown.Periodic.cutoffMassBound: `Breakdown.Periodic.cutoffMassBound` is $\|f\|_2^2\le K/\sqrt{T-t}$ for the cutoff in similarity coordinates and $0<T-t\le1$. Taking square roots and setting $r=1/(8\sqrt{T-t})$ yields the stated growth only for this scaled family with $r\ge1/8$. This linked statement addresses only the $L^2$ estimate. The gradient-error bound is the other assertion in the numbered display.
